title: Euclid’s view of the Dorado group of galaxies
caption: The Dorado group of galaxies, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: Dorado group, NGC 1549, NGC 1553 · constellation Dorado · about 62 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: Part of Euclid’s Early Release Observations, May 2024 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Galaxies are caught in the act of interacting in this Euclid view, trailing tidal tails and shells of stars. They belong to the Dorado group, one of the richest groups of galaxies in the southern sky, about 62 million light-years away in the constellation Dorado.

Dorado is much younger than big clusters such as Fornax. Some of its galaxies are still forming stars, while others seem to have merged fairly recently. In size it falls between large galaxy clusters and small groups, which makes it a useful test of how galaxies grow and collide inside halos of dark matter.

The image spans galaxies from very bright to very faint. Euclid’s wide, sharp view lets one instrument study features as small as star clusters, the centers of galaxies, and long merger tails all at once. Astronomers are using it to catalog globular clusters around the galaxies and to hunt for new dwarf galaxies.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (41 × 41 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 62 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 740,000 × 740,000 light-years. Its light set out about 62 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: The image comes from about an hour of observing. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
alt: Several bright galaxies with faint shells and tidal tails, spread across a dark field of stars and tiny distant galaxies.
